I was just curious as to whether or not people think there should be an
obligation to speak out when there's a rules violations (both a "moral" view
and an official, tournament view).

For example, I'm sure lots of you have come upon situations where the game that
you're playing (or watching) has a minor rules violation. When do you think
it's an obligation to remind the other person and when do you think it's a case
of "too bad, so sad"? Let me illustrate with some examples:

#1. Once in a game, one of my vampires was assaulted by Tutu with a Meat Hook.
I got hit for 3, he pressed, and then got hit for another 3. Now the other
player was under the interpretation that Meat Hook only grants you one press
each combat (whereas it gives a press each time you strike with it). So since
the other player didn't read the card text carefully, I didn't say a word and
combat ended. Should I have said anything? (Or not? It's not *my* fault he
didn't read the card!). (Tangent question: Meat Hook grants an optional
press you strike at close and it isn't dodged right? So if you attack with a
Meat Hook and hit, and then take two additionals and hit again, you have 3
optional presses to continue? Hmmm...).

#2. I'm in a game where my grandpredator is in combat with my predator. My
grandpredator has a vamp with 6 blood, my predator has a vamp with 5 blood.
Each strikes with hands (so 5 and 4 now). And my predator then plays a
Lightning Reflexes for 5 additional strikes (which was good since it torporized
my predator's vamp). Should I felt an obligation to remind everything that
Lightning Reflexes could only have provided 4 additionals (1 + X)? Or is okay
to feign ignorance and since no one else remembered to read the text?

#3. I'm watching a game (I've been ousted) where one of one player's key vamps
is down to 2 blood. During his untap phase, he burns Jake Washington to bring
that vamp up to 6 blood. Should I have made an offhand remark to remind him
that Jake only works on an empty vampire?

In all of the above cases, even if you *should* speak up (if you believe so),
there's really no way to prove you did anything wrong by not speaking up!
(Since you could feign ignorance or sometime afterwards you can "remember" the
right text). And in particular, if you're not in the game, you're supposed to
call a judge but that may be problematic if you constantly see problems and are
calling over a judge every 5 minutes or so. And everyone always hates kibitzers
of course!!!

Furthermore, to sort of "justify" not speaking out, I think it's sort of okay
because it balances all the times when you *know* the correct ruling but
everyone else (including the judge) does things incorrectly. I've had cases
when I was unable to convince people that Thetmes and Regina were titled, that
Tomb of Ramses only gains counters when transfers are made to *that* vampire
(as opposed to any of their other vampires), or you can't Psyche! after
Illusions of the Kindred.

So...any thoughts or stories about when you did or did not remind people of a
ruling?

Halcyan 2

P.S. An additional two questions, as well:

#1. In a previous tournament report (the EC I believe), the judge mentioned
that in the final, someone forgot to pay for contesting and was forced to yield
the vampire (instead of allowing him to pay the pool). Can you do this?

"The cost to contest a card is one pool, which you pay during each of your
untap phases. Instead of paying the cost to contest the card, you may choose to
yield the card. A yielded card is burned. Any cards or counters stacked on the
yielded card are also burned."

Instead of simply being *forced* to yield, shouldn't the person be allowed to
retroactively make the choice? I mean otherwise, I'd play with Society of
Leopolds, and if my prey moved to their Master phase without burning a blood
I'd say "Aha! That means you have to burn the vampire!" I mean, shouldn't all
of these cases sort of mirror Arika's ruling?

"Arika's Prey cannot end her untap phase if she controls a location that she
hasn't burned a pool for, even if she gained control of that location sometime
during her untap phase. [LSJ 19990405]"

So you can't end your untap phase without paying to contest or yielding? Or...?

#2. I know that you aren't allowed to hide or misrepresent any public
information, but are you allowed to hide any cards that aren't supposed to be
there in the first place? For example, Archon and Praxis Seizures go into ash
heap when played but people may keep them on the vamp as reminders. Or if
someone plays a Rider Clause, he/she may keep the card "in play" as a reminder
even though it should go to the ash heap. So...if I play one of those cards and
someone insists that I "keep it in play as a reminder," am I allowed to hide
the card? Is there anything wrong with hiding the Praxis Seizure: Seattle card
under Gideon? If anyone asks about his Princedom, of course I'll answer. But
since the card shouldn't actually be in play in the first place, this really
isn't hiding/misrepresenting public info, is it?

Thanks!

If I understand this correctly, the problem here is not that a rules violation
occurred, just that the other player didn't use his optional press that you would
normally have expected him to use for a reason you didn't understand..._probably_,
but not necessarily, because he didn't understand the card correctly. In this
situation, I would likely speak up in an informal game and may or may not choose
to in a tournament game. I often do unless it's a high-caliber player who I don't

first eyebrow at anyone else who chose not to speak up.

Since I'm part of the game, I'd feel obligated to speak up and insure the game was
played by the correct rules. I would expect other players to do the same, though
if they failed to I wouldn't sit around interrogating them as to whether their feigned
ignorance was a game or not. 1) I can't read mind; and 2) it's just a game and this
isn't the sort of thing that pisses me off. But for myself, this is not the type
of tactic I'd prefer to win by.

> #3. I'm watching a game (I've been ousted) where one of one player's key vamps

Since I'm not part of the game, I would not. I might mention it to a judge who was
watching the game but I would not interact with the players. This could be seen as
coaching for one thing. I'm even a little uncomfortable telling a judge because I
feel like if one player has "watchers" who speak up every time something illegal
happens that is not is his interests, it's not fair unless all the players have
watchers. (Or all the watchers are non-partisan in their willingness to speak up.)
I dislike unfair games as much or more than I dislike seeing minor rules violations
take place, even if they have significant consequences.

> P.S. An additional two questions, as well:
>
> #1. In a previous tournament report (the EC I believe), the judge mentioned
> that in the final, someone forgot to pay for contesting and was forced to yield
> the vampire (instead of allowing him to pay the pool). Can you do this?

That's a technical question I'll leave to the experts...

> #2. I know that you aren't allowed to hide or misrepresent any public

> even though it should go to the ash heap. So...if I play one of those cards and
> someone insists that I "keep it in play as a reminder," am I allowed to hide
> the card?

Well, first of all, someone can't "insist that you keep it in play as a reminder".
If you're doing the legal thing, how can anyone force you to do anything else?
If you do choose to keep it out in front of you (it still technically counts as
being in your ash heap or out of the game, as appropriate, under any circumstances),
I don't see the issue with you dictating the terms involved. If they don't care
for those terms, just put the card wherever it physically belongs and go on.

Fred

inclined to forgive any player that isn't aware... once.

I would probably ask 'Do you want to press?'. If he answers 'No.' so be it.
If he answers 'I don't have any presses', I think I would clue him in that
he does indeed have a press. This way, I am not taking advantage of his
ignorance so much as assuming that he does not *want* to press.

This isn't a matter of sportsmanship--the rules are being violated (albeit
in ignorance).

I would definitely chime in and let them know, in as unobtrusive a way as
possible (and probably piss them all off anyway).

bring

Same as #2. A rule is being violated and this should not be allowed.
However, nine times out of ten it is probably innocent and therefore not
worth a hassle. Merely reading off the text of the card should be
sufficient.

Of course, you're also not in the game any more. Is it your business?
Yeah... I think so, but some would disagree. You'll probably piss someone
off by saying something but since the rules are being broken, I don't think
anyone will complain too loudly.

> In all of the above cases, even if you *should* speak up (if you believe
so),

opinion.

Feigning ignorance is the wrong thing to do IMHO but calling a judge over
would be excessive and rather busy-bodyish. The rules are probably being
broken in an innocent way and the player probably won't appreciate you
'telling' on them. Given a choice between a friendly reminder of card text
by you or possible sanctions from the judge, I'm sure they'd rather have the
former.

Maybe without specifying the error made saying something like "Sorry to
interrupt guys, but I've noticed that you've inadvertently broken the game
rules. Would you rather that I pointed it out or should I not get
involved?". This doesn't blame any one player and gives them the opportunity
to decide for themselves what input they will allow.

Having said that, I generally just play these things by ear. I make a lot of
mistakes myself though and if I were in their position, I would appreciate a
kind reminder.

vampire
> (as opposed to any of their other vampires), or you can't Psyche! after

If someone forgets to place a Temptation counter on my vampire, it's their
own damn fault. If someone forgets that their vampire is actually supposed
to be untapped, I don't care. Optional effects are up to the player to
remember... it's not my job to inform them and it may be to my disadvantage
to remind them. No rules are being broken by remaining silent in that case.
I may even remind someone that they should grab a pool if I don't want them
ousted.

Cheers,
WES

my prey last turn. My predator was debating with HIS predator out-loud

of an extra 2VP. And you can't take back words once they're said, no
matter how many times you say "oops, sorry". So if you're watching a
game and see a misplay; CORK IT!

matter whether you're a player or watcher, you should point it out, ...
no matter what the effect would be. (If you're a watcher, maybe you
should grab the judge to confirm first).

the prey of a Lasombra stealth/bleed deck, played by a person who shall
remain nameless to protect the guilty =). He had been bleeding me
pretty heavily all game, though I was bloating with a speed almost to
match (as well as drawing very close to ousting my own prey). My
predator attempted to play Slaughtering the Herd on his predator with
Ignacio, who lacked superior Dominate, and before I noticed, they had
announced a block attempt and played a stealth card, and a debate about
intercept or rush or something was taking place.

it out; I had to turn to LSJ (who was conveniently standing behind me)

So yes, even when it's totally in your best interest to simply let
things go wrong, you MUST speak up. Otherwise, you've cheated,

Actually, I strongly disagree with that. Games can be about completely
different skills or whatever combination of skills the designers believe
has merit. One thing I think is very bad, however, is to allow some peripheral
skill to creep in around the margins and make a difference. This is because
if I don't happen to like parlour games about making up rhymes on the spot,
I can choose a game that doesn't involve such skills. But if the designers
insist on adding a single card which injects that skill into the flow of
certain games, all of sudden I have to decide whether to tolerate a small
amount of it or abandon an otherwise excellent (IMO) game altogether. It
just isn't worth people having to make that decision just so you can print
ONE SINGLE cutesy parlour-game card.

By the same token, juggling large amounts of detailed information is precisely
a skill I find boring and better left to computers - or at least papers and
pens, which are very good tools we have readily at hand to deal with such
problems. Simulating what human beings can do without a paper and pencil at
hand is not a good subject for a game, IMO. If it spins your buttons, there's
always chess. But if we're going to make it a necessary skill for Jyhad, we
might as well go whole hog and then the people who enjoy it can take it up with
a vengeance and I can move on to games I'll like better.

If you see the parallel here to a certain card here, take note. By making
this argument about the game including the skill of juggling detailed information
in your head, I claim it's also completely fair to include rhyming in that game.
If so, you're also making Andrew's argument for him!

Fred

Assume at the start of my minion phase that I have Hugo out with 2 blood
on him; that my prey has a tapped, full Aabbt Kindred and an untapped,
full Khalil Anvari; and that my predator has an untapped, freshly
influenced Black Cat, and a torporized Uma Hatch. My hand consists of:

Potence skill card
Bum's Rush
Legal Manipulations
Torn Signpost
Immortal Grapple
Undead Strength
Pushing the Limit

A -WIDE- variety of actions are open to me, and which action I take is
totally dependent on my analysis of a LARGE amount of detailed
information.

If I bleed with the Legal Manip, I'll be blocked by Khalil for sure, and
could even be blocked by the Dear Abby if he Wakes. I can kill either
vampire easily with 3 cards; but I'll need to use my IG, because they
both have Presence. If I kill the Dear Abby (or if I kill Khalil with
only 2 cards), I'll be on zero blood and have to hunt next turn; but the
Dear Abby is probably more critical than Khalil. If I draw into a Taste
of Vitae, it doesn't matter, since I'll get all the blood back and fill
Hugo up anyway, but that's a risk.

If I only bleed for one, Khalil could just play Ecstasy and reduce the
bleed; that would be a wasted action, but the Legal Manip is going to be
a wasted card if I use it - save the card, or force him to get in a
fight? At least I don't have to worry about Deflection.

I could just Bum's Rush, but I can't guarantee getting into combat with
the Dear Abby; he might sacrifice Khalil. It might be more worth it to
kill Khalil, but I haven't seen much of his deck yet.

I could always Rush my predator. Both vampires have pre/cel, so odds
seem good that it's some sort of bleed-and-whatever deck. But I don't
have any maneuvers, and if Black Cat has a maneuver, then I've wasted
the Rush card. And Celerity is very likely to have maneuvers. I could
just ignore Black Cat since she'll probably rescue Uma next turn, but do
I want that to happen?

I could hunt. That seems like a waste of time, though it does get some
blood back on Hugo. I could also stay untapped to block Black Cat if
she decides to bleed, although that also seems like a waste of time.

...As you can see, the amount of detailed information required just to
take ONE MINION ACTION is a whole hell of a lot more than you realize.
[0]

Forgetting that Khalil can play Ecstasy, for example, could make you try
bleeding for 1, wanting to save the card for later. Forgetting that the
Dear Abby can prevent 1 point of damage might lead you to play the
Undead Strength instead of Pushing the Limit, or if you notice in time,
you still might not have wanted Hugo to be hunting next turn.

V:TES already requires the skill of juggling detailed information in
your head. It's part and parcel of the game. So it's perfectly
reasonable to expect someone to remember to put Temptation counters on
their card by themselves.

Yes, it is. You're just not looking at it that way.

For example, transient information: last time Alice got into combat
with one of Bob's vampires, Bob played Trap, Inner Essence, Horrid Form,
and Kraken's Kiss, with the resulting rude surprise for Alice's vampire.

Alice can remember one bit of information, "last time I picked a fight
with Bob, my vampire bit the dust", two bits of information "he used
some crazy-ass Trap combat", or multiple bits of information (each card
as it was played and what happened as a result). The more transient
information Alice can successfully remember, the better she's going to
do next time she gets in a fight with Bob; for example, she might
realize that Caliban may LOOK empty, but Inner Essence will let him
still play the above combo.

Transient details, permanent details. Sure, some are a bit harder to
remember. But you have to remember as many as possible, and it really IS
possible to reduce things to chunks in this fashion. It also works very
well for strategy games like this one.

computerized a la Magic. I'd expect the computer version to have reminders for

if you wanted to add a counter or not. Little box would pop up asking if you

small, too big, too similar to other stuff on the table, pushed too far back,

greater problem than people used to playing sloppily.

There are of course situations that come up where one is *forced* into
certain moves, usually involving mandatory moves to protect the King until
one is mated. In such a situation, one would be able to safely say "Mate in
three".

Aside from that though, there would be no way of logically determining how
many moves ahead you can calculate. Since each new move changes the
paramaters of the board, you couldn't accurately plan unless you could also
accurately determine your (human) opponent's each and every move. This would
not require logic... it would require Telepathy (or superior Auspex--there,
made it Jyhad related :)

Determining a computer's each and every move would of course be much easier
since it would be following the logic it was programmed with... I guess. I
don't claim to be an expert programmer. I imagine that 'randomness' (as
random as you *can* be with a computer...) could be used to change the
'difficulty' of the computer you are playing against. Give it a 20% chance
of making a stupid move for example...

Another factor which I assume would be problematic for a Chess program is
determining value of pieces. The standard values associated with each piece
do not take into account their position on the board. So, while a Pawn is
worth only 1 point, a Pawn which is one move away from becoming a Queen
should be worth much more. A Pawn which is about to be promoted, but which
is threatened by another piece would detract from its value. It gets more
complicaed from there. Creating a true value system for this would be
problematic to say the least.

Kind of like saying Gratiano is worth 8 points but a Gratiano who is in
torpor, with a Disarm on him, with a Derangement on him and empty of blood
is worth a hell of a lot less... ok, I'm stretching this with inane Jyhad
examples but fuck it, I'm interested in this discussion.

whole snotload of other figures and calculations that I do not
comprehend entirely. They then use those values to determine the
"value" of move lines by computing future values of pieces/squares, and
select the liness that increase their own pieces' future values by the
most.

How they do this, I have no idea. My own brain substitutes a ridiculous
amount of pattern-recognition skillz for it.

>do not take into account their position on the board. So, while a Pawn is
>worth only 1 point, a Pawn which is one move away from becoming a Queen
>should be worth much more. A Pawn which is about to be promoted, but which
>is threatened by another piece would detract from its value. It gets more
>complicaed from there. Creating a true value system for this would be
>problematic to say the least.

This goes back to the bit earlier; it's almost IMPOSSIBLE to teach a
computer what the value of a certain square is. But in a great number
of games, c4/c5/f4/f5 end up being extremely important to control, even
though no pieces are actually present on the square during the battle
over it. The "hole" in a Stonewall position is extremely important, for
example; deny your opponent the opportunity to station a Knight on the
hole and you severely cripple his hopes of offense.
